prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You could drive out of this country and attack the world with your ambition, invent wonder plasmas, become an artist of the provocative gesture, the suggestive nod, you could leave wanting the world and return carrying it, a noisy bundle of steam and libido, a ball of fire balanced on your tongue, you might reclaim Main Street in a limo longer than a sermon, wave at our red faces while remembering that you were born a clod hopper, a farmer’s kid, and get over that hump once and for all by telling A Great Man’s stories— the dirty jokes of dictators, tidbits of presidential hygiene, insights into the psychotropic qualities of power and the American tradition of kissing moneyed ass. Your uncle would still call you Roy Boy, pheasants sun themselves beside the tracks, waiting for the dew to burn off before their first flight, and corn grow so high that if you stood in the field you’d disappear, the fact aiming your eyes down the road.

- The person might return triumphantly, displaying wealth, power, and success to the people of Main Street.

Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The passage explores ambition, reinvention, and the desire to escape rural origins through a lyrical, hyperbolic vision of worldly success and proximity to power. It ultimately suggests that no amount of achievement can fully erase one’s beginnings, making home and identity persistent forces beneath public triumph.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Main, Street

outputs.L1: You could drive out of this country and assault the world with your ambition; invent wondrous plasmas; become an artist of the provocative gesture, the suggestive nod. You could leave wanting the world and return carrying it: a noisy bundle of steam and libido, a ball of fire balanced on your tongue. You might reclaim Main Street in a limousine longer than a sermon, waving at our red faces while remembering that you were born a clodhopper, a farmer’s kid, and get over that hump once and for all by telling A Great Man’s stories—the dirty jokes of dictators, tidbits of presidential hygiene, insights into the psychotropic qualities of power and the American tradition of kissing moneyed ass. Your uncle would still call you Roy Boy; pheasants would sun themselves beside the tracks, waiting for the dew to burn off before their first flight; and corn would grow so high that, if you stood in the field, you’d disappear—the fact aiming your eyes down the road.
outputs.L2: You might leave this nation by car and hurl your ambition at the rest of the world; you might devise miraculous plasmas, make yourself into a master of the daring gesture and the loaded glance. You could depart hungry for everything and come back as if you had gathered the whole globe in your arms—a loud knot of vapor and desire, a flame poised on your tongue. Maybe you would roll back onto Main Street in a limousine stretched longer than a preacher’s lesson, lifting a hand to our flushed faces, all while recalling that you began life as a clodhopper, a farmer’s child. And perhaps you would finally climb past that old shame by recounting the tales of A Great Man: the obscene humor of tyrants, small details about presidents’ cleanliness, lessons on the mind-altering nature of authority, and on the American habit of groveling before wealth. Still, your uncle would go on calling you Roy Boy. Pheasants would continue to warm themselves near the railroad tracks, waiting for the morning wetness to vanish before they took their first flight. The corn would rise so tall that a person standing among the stalks would be swallowed from sight, and that knowledge would pull your gaze toward the road ahead.
outputs.L3:
The passage imagines a person leaving a rural home behind in order to pursue vast worldly ambitions and extraordinary creative achievement. From a modest beginning, perhaps as the child of a farmer, this person sets out into the wider world seeking recognition, influence, and success. Their dreams are not small: they long to create, to conquer, to rise above the limitations of their birthplace, and to prove themselves among powerful people and celebrated figures.

The text also imagines the possibility of a triumphant return. Having gained wealth, status, and authority, the person might come back to Main Street in a display of success. They may return with visible signs of power—fine clothes, money, accomplishments, and stories of important places and important men. To the people who remained behind, such a return might appear impressive, even dazzling. It would seem to confirm that the person had escaped ordinary life and achieved something grand.

Yet the passage suggests that this outward triumph cannot erase the person’s origins. No matter how far they travel or how high they rise, they remain shaped by the rural world that produced them. Their identity as a farmer’s child is not something they can simply discard. Beneath the wealth, ambition, and public success, the memory of their humble beginnings continues to define them. The fields, the family, and the habits of rural life remain part of who they are.

In this way, the passage critiques the pursuit of status for its own sake. It questions the value of trying to become important merely by standing close to power, accumulating wealth, or associating oneself with the stories of famous men. Such achievements may impress others, but they do not necessarily provide true greatness or inner fulfillment. The text implies that worldly recognition can be superficial when it is disconnected from self-knowledge, memory, and genuine human ties.

Ultimately, the rural landscape and family connections serve as grounding forces. They remind the ambitious person of where they came from and of the life that existed before fame or fortune. Main Street, the farm, and the family home remain symbols of origin, truth, and belonging. However far the person may go, these roots persist, quietly challenging any attempt to build an identity solely on ambition, prestige, or public success.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents ambition as both a driving force and a kind of dream, imagining success in extravagant, almost mythic terms. Its speaker looks beyond rural origins toward a larger, more dazzling world of influence, wealth, sophistication, and recognition. The desire to rise is not modest or practical; it is lyrical and hyperbolic, filled with images of grand achievement and closeness to powerful people. Success is imagined not simply as comfort or security, but as transformation: a way of becoming someone new, someone admired, someone far removed from the limitations and obscurity of home.

At the same time, the passage suggests that reinvention is never complete. However far a person travels, and however impressive their public triumphs may become, their beginnings remain part of them. Rural life, family history, and early identity continue to exist beneath the polished surface of worldly success. The speaker may dream of escape, but the language of the passage implies that home is not merely a place one leaves behind; it is a force that shapes memory, desire, and self-understanding. In this way, the passage balances aspiration with inevitability. It celebrates the intoxicating fantasy of rising above one’s circumstances, while also recognizing that origins cannot be entirely erased. Public achievement may change how a person is seen by others, but it cannot fully sever the deeper ties of identity, memory, and belonging.
outputs.L5:
**You Belong on Main Street**

Main Street is more than just a place on a map. It is where community, connection, and everyday life come together. Whether you are visiting a local shop, meeting a friend for coffee, or taking a quiet walk through town, Main Street offers something familiar and welcoming.

When you spend time on Main Street, you support local businesses, discover unique places, and become part of the neighborhood’s story. Every storefront, café, and corner has its own character, making Main Street a special destination for residents and visitors alike.

You do not need a special reason to explore Main Street. Sometimes the best moments happen when you simply slow down, look around, and enjoy what is right in front of you. Main Street is where memories are made, traditions continue, and communities grow stronger.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, lyrical paragraph in second person about a rural Midwestern farm boy named Roy who dreams of leaving home, becoming powerful and worldly, and returning triumphantly, in a maximalist literary style.
counterfactuals.output: You are Roy, farm boy of the middle country, child of cornlight and dust, born where the gravel roads run straight as commandments between fields that lift and fall under weather like the breathing of some green, indifferent god, and all your life you have stood at the edge of your father’s acreage with burrs in your socks and sunburn on your neck, listening to the world beyond the section lines call in a language made of train whistles, contrails, radio static, and the glossy murmur of cities you have never seen but have imagined so fiercely they seem less like places than prophecies: towers with windows bright as stacked coins, avenues wet with neon, restaurants where silverware shines like surgical instruments, rooms where men in black suits speak softly and are obeyed, ports, airports, capitals, hotels with marble lobbies, banks with brass doors, women smelling of rain and violets, newspapers unfolding your name like a flag. You are Roy, who rises before dawn to feed hogs steaming in their pens, who shoulders sacks of seed, who drives the tractor through the long afternoons while the sky piles itself with thunderheads like white empires, who knows the ache of rope-burn and baling wire, the sour-sweet breath of cattle, the Sunday sting of soap behind the ears, the way your mother’s hands look in dishwater, red and capable, the way your father’s silence sits at the kitchen table heavier than any grace; and yet inside you something jeweled and ravenous turns and turns, a bright machinery of wanting, grinding the homely facts of your life into fuel. You dream not merely of leaving but of departing, of vanishing one morning past the silo and the mailbox and the school bus stop as though into legend, carrying a cardboard suitcase, a few dollars, a clean shirt, and that secret furnace behind your ribs; you dream of the county shrinking behind you, the water tower, the church steeple, the feed mill, the cracked diamond of the ball field, all receding into a miniature arrangement of pity and tenderness, while ahead the rails or highway fling themselves toward consequence. In your mind you educate yourself in the alphabets of power: cuff links, foreign currencies, maps pinned with red flags, cigars glowing in rooms paneled with dark wood, signatures that move money, handshakes that alter weather, photographs taken from below so that your jaw appears carved from public stone; you practice in the barn mirror the face you will wear when you have become worldly, impenetrable, magnanimous, a man who can order wine without looking at the list, who can pronounce the names of distant cities without blushing, who knows how to lean from a balcony above traffic and feel nothing like fear. But beneath all that hunger is the deeper theater, the homecoming you rehearse while the locusts shrill in August and the soybeans silver under wind: you will return, Roy, not as the boy who left with manure on his boots and chaff in his hair, but transfigured, burnished, carrying the far world on your shoulders like a cloak; you will arrive in a car so dark and polished it will hold the whole farm upside down in its doors, and the dogs will bark uncertainly, and the neighbors will pause at their windows, and your mother will come onto the porch wiping her hands on her apron, and your father, older now, diminished perhaps by time or perhaps only by the grandeur of your arrival, will stand in the yard with his cap in one hand, squinting as if into weather. You imagine stepping out slowly, the prodigal not begging forgiveness but dispensing it, your shoes unmarked by mud, your coat cut in a city where no one has ever heard coyotes at night, your voice deepened by travel, tobacco, command; and you will look upon the fields that once seemed to imprison you and see them transformed into inheritance, origin, mythic loam, the dark Midwestern earth from which you, Roy, rose like a rumor of empire. You will buy the farm, perhaps, or save it, or let it stand merely as proof that you were once small enough to be contained by fences; you will pay the church roof fund, endow the school library, shake the hands of men who once called you reckless, smile gently at girls who married other boys, speak kindly to the clerk who miscounted change, leave large bills under coffee cups, and everywhere your name will move ahead of you like weather: Roy has come back, Roy made good, Roy went out into the world and returned with it in his pocket. Yet even in the dream, even at its most golden and cinematic, when sunset lays its molten law across the barns and the cottonwoods stir like applause and the entire township seems to kneel in the amber dust of your vindication, there is still the boy in you standing barefoot on the cooling porch boards, looking beyond the fields to the place where the road thins into blue distance, still aching, still listening, still unable to tell whether the thing you want is conquest or escape, applause or absolution, the world’s astonished envy or simply a life large enough that the sky above your father’s farm will no longer feel like a lid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, poetic passage that sounds like contemporary American literary fiction, mixing small-town imagery, ambition, politics, money, sex, and the fantasy of escape from a farming background.
counterfactuals.output:
By August the corn stood higher than the mailbox and the whole town seemed to breathe through it, a green lung rustling under the power lines. At night the elevators blinked red above the co-op like some distant city we’d been promised if we behaved, if we kept our hands out of our pockets and our names out of the paper. Men in seed caps talked ethanol and school-board taxes beneath the fluorescent hum of the Casey’s, their faces shiny with weather and grievance, while the women moved through the aisles with checkbooks, coupons, prescriptions, histories of silence.

I wanted out the way a body wants air underwater. I wanted money first, then beauty, then the kind of address nobody could picture accurately. I wanted a room in a tall building where no one knew my father’s debts or my mother’s maiden name, where desire arrived clean as room service and left before breakfast. But in town every appetite had a witness. The banker’s son kissed me behind the Legion after a fundraiser for a man who called himself pro-family and smelled like bourbon and new leather. The candidate shook hands with farmers ruined by markets he’d never seen, promising relief in the language of weather: soon, soon, soon.

All spring my father planted into mud, saying a man could do everything right and still lose the farm, as if this were wisdom and not an indictment. The subsidy checks came late. The auction bills came early. My mother watched the news with one hand on her throat, senators blooming on the screen like mold. I lay awake in my childhood bed beneath the quilt of blue stars, imagining highways unspooling west, imagining my own life as something glossy and wicked and paid for in cash. Outside, the hog barns glowed under the moon, and the air was thick with manure, lilac, diesel—proof that everything we tried to rise above had already entered us, sweetly, permanently, through the mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a pastiche of a postmodern novel about a young man from Main Street imagining himself conquering the world, full of extravagant metaphors, satire of American ambition, and rural details.
counterfactuals.output:
On Main Street, which was not so much a street as a sentence America kept writing in gravel and chewing gum, the young man stood outside the feed store and imagined the world kneeling.

His name was Caleb, though in his private dispatches he called himself C. Augustus Flint, Emperor of All Noon, Chairman of the Weather, First Shareholder in the Moon. He was twenty-two, narrow-shouldered, and possessed of that most dangerous rural inheritance: a view of the horizon unblocked by buildings. Every morning he watched the sun rise over soybean fields like a corporate logo unveiling itself in gold, and every morning he took this as a personal memo from destiny.

Main Street had six storefronts, three of them empty, one of them selling bait, one of them selling insurance against catastrophes too local to interest God, and one of them selling pie. The town’s prosperity had departed years before in a refrigerated truck, leaving behind a bank sign, a water tower, and a festival celebrating a crop nobody grew anymore. Yet Caleb loved it with the guilty tenderness of a conqueror inspecting the village he would later burn for symbolism.

He had plans.

Not ordinary plans, like getting certified in HVAC or marrying a girl from church whose laugh sounded like screen doors in June. No. Caleb’s plans were architectural, imperial, laminated in the mind. He would begin, naturally, with an app.

The app would connect people who wanted things with people who had things, which Caleb understood to be the entire secret engine of civilization. It would disrupt the county fair, then groceries, then loneliness, then death. Investors would arrive by helicopter, descending upon the high school football field in Italian shoes, carrying briefcases fat with venture capital and spiritual emptiness. They would sit with him at Donna’s Diner beneath the mounted bass and ask, “Caleb, how did you see what none of us could see?”

And Caleb would point through the window at the grain elevator, that white cathedral of corn, and say, “Gentlemen, I listened to America breathing.”

In truth, America wheezed. It wheezed through the dryers at the laundromat, through the busted mufflers outside the Dollar General, through the old men at the co-op discussing rain as if weather were a declining stock. It wheezed in patriotic bunting faded to the color of old bruises. It wheezed in the courthouse clock, which had been ten minutes slow since 1978 and was locally admired for its consistency.

But Caleb heard trumpets.

He walked Main Street with his earbuds in and saw, not cracked sidewalks tufted with crabgrass, but avenues of conquest. The barber pole became a lance. The stoplight, blinking red at midnight, became the eye of history. The smell of manure from the fairgrounds rose in his nostrils as incense from the altars of expansion. Even the flies seemed like black punctuation marks in the epic he was composing around himself.

At night he sat in his mother’s trailer, beneath a ceiling stain shaped like Florida, and drafted manifestos on a laptop missing the G key. His mother worked double shifts at the nursing home and came home smelling of antiseptic, mashed potatoes, and other people’s endings. She would find him at the kitchen table surrounded by energy drink cans, scribbling arrows between words like PLATFORM, SCALE, DOMINATE, and LEGACY.

“You eat today?” she would ask.

“History doesn’t eat,” Caleb said once.

His mother looked at him for a long moment, then set a plate of meatloaf beside his elbow. “History can microwave that if it gets hungry.”

This was the sort of remark Caleb intended to omit from his memoirs.

His memoirs, already titled *From Dust to Dominion*, would begin in the third person, shift without warning into deposition transcript, then include several blank pages to symbolize the years when no one believed in him. There would be a chapter composed entirely of receipts. Critics would call it “a savage indictment of capital and cornbread.” Caleb had never read critics, but he imagined they wore scarves and trembled easily.

He had learned ambition from television, from presidents, from halftime speeches, from the bright sermons of billionaires who claimed to have started with nothing except a garage, a father’s loan, and a childhood free from medical debt. He had absorbed the national catechism: Wanting is virtue. Winning is proof. The self is a frontier, and every frontier is improved by extraction.

So he extracted. From the town, he extracted symbols. From his mother, patience. From his friends, unpaid labor. From the county library, books about leadership he did not return. From himself, a feverish belief that if he could become enormous enough, no one would notice how small he felt when the wind moved through the corn at night like a crowd whispering his real name.

There was a girl, because empires require witnesses. Her name was Mara. She worked at the seed dealership and had the practical beauty of someone who knew how to change a tire in church clothes. Caleb told her one evening by the old railroad tracks that he intended to conquer the world.

“The whole thing?” she asked.

“Eventually.”

“What about Canada?”

“Phase Two.”

She nodded toward a ditch where frogs were screaming in the wet grass. “You might start with your student loans.”

Caleb smiled sadly, as prophets do when confronted by municipal accounting.

He tried to explain the scale of his vision. He told her Main Street was merely a launchpad, that the town’s rusted silos were rockets in disguise, that the cattle lowing beyond the auction barn were a chorus of ancient shareholders demanding growth. He spoke of markets as if they were weather systems, of branding as if it were baptism, of success as if it were a country where nobody ever had to apologize.

Mara listened, picking burrs from her sleeve.

“You ever think,” she said, “that maybe the world doesn’t want conquering?”

This was, Caleb felt, the kind of sentence that kept people in towns with one stoplight.

Still, it followed him home. It rode in the passenger seat past the Cenex sign and the cemetery and the little white church with its marquee reading GOD HAS A PLAN, which Caleb always considered useful confirmation but poor branding. The sentence sat beside him while crickets sawed the darkness into planks. It watched as he opened his laptop and stared at a blinking cursor, that tiny metronome of judgment.

Maybe the world did not want conquering.

Maybe the world wanted fixing, or feeding, or to be left alone in its field under the indifferent stars. Maybe Main Street, with its potholes and pie case and veterans’ memorial and gossip moving faster than broadband, was not a prison but a paragraph. Maybe ambition was a tractor stuck in mud: the more wildly the wheels spun, the deeper it sank.

Caleb rejected this thought immediately and replaced it with a five-year plan.

By winter, his app had three users: himself, a retired gym teacher, and a bot offering discounted sunglasses. He held strategy meetings in the closed video rental store, whose shelves still bore labels—COMEDY, HORROR, WESTERN—as if all human endeavor could be alphabetized and rented for three nights. He paced beneath fluorescent lights while snow pressed its blank face against the windows.

“We are pre-revenue,” he told his reflection.

His reflection, pale and overcaffeinated, seemed pre-everything.

Outside, Main Street endured. Pickup trucks coughed awake. The plow buried everyone’s mailbox with democratic efficiency. Farmers in insulated coveralls discussed diesel prices with the grim intimacy of surgeons. At Donna’s, the pie rotated according to a calendar more reliable than Congress. The town did not kneel. The world did not kneel. Even Caleb’s dog, Jackson, refused to sit unless shown the treat first.

And yet—here the narrator, who has been loitering behind the grain elevator with a notebook and questionable motives, must confess a tenderness—there was something magnificent in the boy’s delusion. Not noble, exactly. Not wise. But magnificent in the way a rooster is magnificent, declaring sovereignty over a yard owned by the bank.

For what was America, if not Caleb writ large? A country standing on its own Main Street, pockets full of borrowed money, announcing to the cornfields that it had been chosen. A country forever mistaking appetite for destiny, noise for music, expansion for grace. A country looking at every horizon and seeing not distance, not mystery, but inventory.

Spring came. The fields darkened. The ditches filled with meltwater and beer cans. Caleb walked to the edge of town where Main Street gave up and became County Road 9, then gravel, then dust. He stood there as the wind lifted the smell of turned earth, hog barns, lilac, gasoline, rain.

The world stretched before him, unconquered and unimpressed.

He raised one hand, not quite in farewell, not quite in command.

Somewhere a meadowlark sang like a golden screw coming loose from the machinery of heaven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid literary monologue about leaving one’s country hometown to become a great man, then returning with stories of power and corruption, while still being haunted by farm life and family nicknames.
counterfactuals.output:
I left home because the fields were too low for my dreams.

That is the grand way to say it, the way men say such things after they have acquired a black coat, a manner of pausing before mirrors, and the habit of being listened to. But the truth is plainer and uglier: I left because I was ashamed of the mud on my boots, ashamed of the sagging barn, ashamed of being called Little Tad by uncles with tobacco in their cheeks and hayseed in their hair. I left because the rooster knew my name and screamed it every morning as if it were a sentence. I left because Ma could holler “Taddy!” from the porch and all of creation—dogs, crows, milk cows, cousins—would turn and know exactly who was meant.

I wanted a name that did not end in laughter.

So I went away.

I took the dawn train with one suitcase, two collars, and a heart stuffed full of thunder. The town slipped behind me: the feed store, the church steeple, the cemetery where our people lay under stones tilted by frost, the creek where we boys baptized one another in sin and algae. I watched the last fence post vanish and swore I would not come back until the world had learned to stand when I entered a room.

And by God, it did.

Or enough of it did to fool me.

In the city I learned the language of doors: which ones open to money, which to women, which to judges, which to rooms where nothing is written down and everything is decided. I learned to shake hands without warmth, to smile without mercy, to call theft policy and cowardice prudence. I dined beneath chandeliers big as frozen lightning. I sat at tables where senators chewed lamb with their soft pink mouths and sold rivers, railroads, boys, borders, futures. I watched fortunes born in the time it took a pen to scratch a name. I watched honest men invited upstairs and carried out ruined.

They called me brilliant.

They called me necessary.

They called me sir.

Not once did they call me Little Tad.

I became the sort of man my hometown would have imagined only in sermons—part example, part warning. My photograph appeared in papers; my enemies lowered their voices; my friends, if that is the word for men who stand near a fire for warmth, multiplied. I had power enough to make a guilty man innocent by breakfast and an innocent one invisible by noon. I saw corruption not as a monster in an alley but as a banquet—well-lit, well-attended, fragrant with roast meat and perfume. No one there had horns. No one cackled. They toasted the republic. They quoted Scripture. They sent flowers to widows they had made.

And I, too, raised my glass.

Do not look at me like that. Ambition has its own weather. You stand in it long enough and you forget what sunshine felt like.

But at night—ah, at night the farm returned.

Not as memory. As visitation.

I would lie in a hotel bed in some capital city, silk sheets cold as water, and hear the barn roof ticking in the summer heat. I would smell manure under the cologne on my wrists. I would see Father bent over a plow horse, his hands cracked like old fence rails, saying nothing, always saying nothing, because men of our blood considered tenderness a crop that failed too often to plant. I would hear my sister Maybelle laughing, calling me Tadpole when I slipped at the well, and my brother Jem shouting, “Run, Little Tad, run!” as the bull came loose and I tore across the pasture with death snorting behind me and everyone, even Ma, laughing from the fence.

Those names stuck in me deeper than any title.

Chairman washed off.

Honorable washed off.

Your Excellency washed off.

But Tadpole remained, slick and squirming in the dark.

And now I have returned, haven’t I? Look at this place. Smaller than sin and twice as stubborn. The road still ruts after rain. The same elm leans over the schoolhouse like an old woman listening for gossip. The post office smells of dust and glue. Boys stare at my motorcar as if it fell from Mars. Old men pretend not to know me, then know me too loudly. Women peer through curtains, measuring the distance between the child I was and the man I have dressed myself to be.

They ask for stories.

So I give them stories.

I tell them of marble halls where men speak of the people and mean themselves. I tell them of governors who tremble before bankers, and bankers who tremble before rumors, and rumors that begin as whispers in bedrooms and end as hunger in counties no map remembers. I tell them of contracts greased with blood, of ballots bought for less than a winter coat, of factories where girls grow old before twenty, of policemen who know which skulls may be cracked without paperwork. I tell them I have seen power naked, and it is not majestic. It is paunchy. It sweats. It fears laughter above all things.

They listen with open mouths, proud that one of their own has walked among devils and learned their Christian names.

They do not ask what I did there.

No one asks that in a hometown. They either know already or love you too much to know.

Ma is gone now. Father too. The porch sags where she used to stand. The barn has caved in on one side, like a beast tired of holding its breath. In the kitchen, the wallpaper still blooms with little blue flowers, faded almost white. I stood there this morning and could nearly hear her: “Taddy, bring in wood.” Not sir. Not mister. Not that grand hard name printed beneath my portrait.

Taddy.

I have crossed oceans of smoke and money to be undone by two syllables.

This is what no one tells you about leaving: you may become great, but you do not become new. The boy you were follows at a distance, barefoot, freckled, carrying a pail, waiting for you to look back. He knows where you buried the kittens. He knows you cried when the mare died. He knows the first lie you told and the first thing you stole and how you prayed one winter night not for virtue, not for salvation, but that the calf with the white blaze would live till morning.

I left to escape the smallness of this place.

But small things have long roots.

A nickname. A fieldstone. A mother’s apron snapping on the line. The sour-sweet smell of silage. The scrape of a hoe. The way dusk gathers in a furrow. These have followed me into mansions and council chambers, into smoke-filled rooms where men decided the price of another man’s life. And sometimes, as I signed my name to some magnificent ruin, I would see my father’s hands in my own and wonder whether the dirt had ever truly come clean.

Now they want me to speak at the church supper. They want the great man to tell the children how to rise.

What shall I tell them?

Leave, yes. Leave if you must. Let the train take you. Let the city sharpen your teeth. Learn the passwords. Wear the fine suit. Climb until the air thins and the men beside you smile like knives.

But remember this: the world will offer you many names, and most of them will be lies.

The true ones wait at home. They wait in the mouths of the dead. They wait in the dust under the bed, in the pasture gone to weed, in the kitchen where nobody calls you anymore.

I wanted to be a great man.

And I became one, if greatness is measured by fear, by reach, by the number of men who curse you quietly and bow when you pass.

But tonight, standing under these country stars—so many, so mercilessly bright—I would trade half my honors to hear Ma call from the porch once more, angry as thunder, loving as bread:

“Little Tad! Supper!”
